zones.name: App Shell
zones.description: Defines the React Router application entry point, global styles, and the top-level route tree that bootstraps the entire client experience.
insights: High cohesion (1) — files are tightly interconnected
Perfect cohesion (1.0) with zero coupling confirms this zone is correctly scoped to bootstrapping concerns only
home.tsx being the sole route handler suggests the app is early-stage or intentionally single-page, leaving room for route expansion into the engine zone
The absence of any inbound cross-zone imports confirms this is a true leaf entry point consumed by the runtime, not by other zones
With only one route (home.tsx), all game rendering is likely delegated immediately to the engine zone, keeping the shell thin and appropriately separated
app.css at the shell level implies global styles are not co-located with components; consider whether component-scoped styles belong in the engine zone instead
Routes exclusively import from the hooks layer (never directly from engine or services), confirming the shell maintains a single-layer dependency contract that is enforced by check-layers.sh
The shell's strict hooks-only import pattern makes it the cleanest enforced boundary in the codebase — no leakage into engine or persistence internals

app-shell → hooks is the only outbound import direction from the shell; routes/play.tsx and routes/worlds.tsx import exclusively from ~/hooks, making the hooks layer a true anti-corruption layer between the UI entry point and domain logic

The app-shell zone contains zero test files of its own — the architectural boundary enforcement for routes (hooks-only imports) is delegated entirely to check-layers.sh and zone-boundaries.test.ts in the project-config zone. If a new route file is added that imports directly from the engine or services, no test within the shell zone will catch it before the CI script runs.

The app-shell zone has no co-located tests validating its own import contracts. The hooks-only import rule for route files is enforced by tools outside the zone (check-layers.sh, zone-boundaries.test.ts). A misconfigured route added by a contributor unfamiliar with the layer rules will not surface a failure until CI runs the external script, rather than failing a fast local unit test adjacent to the offending file.

zones.name: Arc Geometry
zones.description: Provides pure geometric calculation utilities for rendering the rainbow arc curve, decoupled from any React or rendering framework concerns.
insights: High cohesion (1) — files are tightly interconnected
A framework-free utility zone with perfect cohesion is the correct pattern for mathematical primitives shared across rendering layers
Both the engine and components zones import from geometry, confirming it serves as a shared foundation rather than a point-to-point helper
Keeping geometry free of React dependencies ensures it remains testable in isolation and portable if the rendering layer ever changes
Zero coupling and pure utility classification make this zone an ideal candidate for unit testing without any rendering harness
Two consumers (engine and components) importing the same geometry file independently could indicate that arc geometry will grow — document its public API surface early to prevent drift

arc-geometry has two independent consumers (engine and rainbow-arc-component) that each import it separately rather than through a single intermediary — any breaking API change in arc-geometry (e.g. renamed export, changed parameter signature) requires coordinated fixes in two separate zones with no shared caller to absorb the change

arc-geometry is consumed independently by both the engine zone and the rainbow-arc-component zone. This fan-out means the geometry module's public API has two callers with no intermediary, so a signature change propagates to two zones simultaneously. As the geometry module grows, documenting and freezing its exported API surface becomes load-bearing for zone stability.

arc-geometry symbols are reachable through three paths from within the codebase: direct import from ~/geometry/rainbow-arc (used by RainbowArc.tsx), re-export through ~/engine barrel (used by useRainbowEasterEgg), and transitively via ~/engine → rainbow-arc-component → geometry — only the first path is semantically correct; the second creates a hidden alias on the engine barrel surface that inflates its apparent API size

The engine barrel re-exports all arc-geometry symbols, creating an undocumented alias: `import { computeArcProgress } from '~/engine'` and `import { computeArcProgress } from '~/geometry/rainbow-arc'` resolve to identical code. This makes the engine barrel appear to own geometry logic it merely proxies. Remove the re-exports from the engine barrel to make the geometry module the sole canonical import source.

zones.name: Build & Deploy Scripts
zones.description: Shell scripts for enforcing architectural layer rules at CI time and for deploying the application.
insights: Isolated files — no import edges between 2 files, cohesion is unmeasurable (reported as 0)
check-layers.sh enforces import-graph layer constraints — keep it wired into CI so layer violations are caught automatically rather than discovered in code review
deploy.sh is a standalone deployment script; verify it has no hardcoded environment-specific values (credentials, project IDs) that should live in CI environment variables instead
With cohesion and coupling both at 0, these scripts are fully self-contained, which is appropriate for infrastructure tooling — no action needed on those metrics
Cohesion of 0 is expected and acceptable for shell scripts, which have no import graph relationships; this metric is not meaningful for this zone.

check-layers.sh and deploy.sh serve distinct concerns (architecture enforcement vs. deployment); grouping them is fine at this codebase size, but they would naturally split into separate CI and infra zones if the scripts directory grows.

check-layers.sh encodes a 6-layer model (geometry → engine → services → hooks → components → routes) that does not map 1-to-1 to the zone model, which has no dedicated hooks or routes zones — layer compliance can be verified by the script but cannot be inferred from zone metrics alone

The scripts zone is the sole authoritative source of the architectural contract; it governs all runtime zones without appearing in the import graph, making it an invisible load-bearing dependency of the entire architecture

The enforced 6-layer DAG in check-layers.sh includes hooks and routes as distinct layers, but the zone model collapses hooks into the engine zone and routes into the app zone — zone cohesion/coupling metrics therefore cannot surface hooks→services or routes→hooks violations; consider aligning zone boundaries with enforced layer boundaries

check-layers.sh is the only artifact that encodes the 6-layer architectural contract, but it is a shell script with no schema or machine-readable format — if the layer names or file-path conventions change, the script silently stops enforcing rather than failing loudly; consider a structured config (e.g. JSON layer manifest) that both the script and zone-boundary tests consume from a single source of truth

The 6-layer DAG contract lives exclusively in an unstructured shell script; layer renames or path convention changes cause silent enforcement gaps rather than explicit failures — extract the layer definitions into a machine-readable config shared by check-layers.sh and zone-boundaries.test.ts

eslint.config.ts declares itself 'the ONE AND ONLY mechanism that enforces the architecture layer boundary at import time' (line 6–8), but check-layers.sh enforces the same DAG redundantly and independently — these two mechanisms are not documented as intentionally redundant, creating ambiguity about which is authoritative when they diverge or when one is disabled

check-layers.sh header comment (line 12) documents that 'components/ must NOT import from routes/' but omits the 'components/ must NOT import from services/' constraint that the script also enforces on line 49 — the header is an incomplete and potentially misleading contract for contributors reading the documentation section only

check-layers.sh line 12 documents only one of the two constraints enforced for the components layer — it mentions 'routes' but silently omits 'services'. A developer reading only the header comment block (lines 5–12) will have an incomplete picture of what is enforced. Update line 12 to: '- components/ must NOT import from routes/ or services/'.

eslint.config.ts claims to be the sole enforcement mechanism but check-layers.sh enforces the same rules — if ESLint is truly the single source of truth, check-layers.sh is redundant and should be documented as a secondary smoke-check rather than an independent enforcer; if both are intentional, eslint.config.ts line 6 should be corrected to say 'primary mechanism' rather than 'ONE AND ONLY'.

useLevelById is the only hook that does not export a Use{HookName}Return interface — it is exported from the barrel (hooks/index.ts:33) without a companion type export, silently breaking the implicit hook return-type naming convention followed by every other hook in the barrel

inventory-shared.ts uses a kebab-case hyphenated name with a -shared suffix that matches no documented naming convention in the codebase — component files are PascalCase, utility files are kebab-case, but the -shared suffix pattern is unique to this file and undocumented, making it non-discoverable for contributors adding a second shared interface file

useLevelById is the only hook without a Use{HookName}Return export type. Add `export type UseLevelByIdReturn = LevelData | undefined` to useLevelById.ts and re-export it through the hooks barrel to complete the convention.

The engine barrel proxies arc-geometry exports (lines 95-104), causing hooks to import geometry constants via ~/engine while RainbowArc.tsx imports them directly from ~/geometry/rainbow-arc. Remove the geometry re-exports from the engine barrel and have all consumers import directly from ~/geometry/rainbow-arc to eliminate the dual-path aliasing.

The engine barrel's HIGH FAN-IN advisory (line 22) instructs contributors to manually grep before modifying exports but is not backed by any automated check. Add a snapshot or import-count assertion to zone-boundaries.test.ts that fails when the number of ~/engine consumers exceeds a documented threshold, converting the prose warning into an enforced constraint.

inventory-shared.ts uses a unique -shared suffix naming pattern with no documented convention. Rename to shared-inventory-types.ts or InventoryShared.ts (matching component or utility conventions respectively) and document the chosen pattern for future shared-type files.

The save-persistence zone is the only zone with both cohesion below 0.4 (0.36) and coupling above 0.6 (0.64). Cohesion is 0.36 (below the 0.4 threshold), indicating the hook and service files are not tightly interrelated by imports — splitting useSave into the App Shell zone would raise cohesion and clarify layer boundaries.
Coupling is 0.64 (above the 0.6 threshold), driven by 9 imports from the Game Engine — the engine should depend on a narrow, stable interface rather than importing broadly from this zone.
services/index.ts acting as a barrel entrypoint is a good encapsulation pattern; ensure it is the only import path the engine uses so internal restructuring doesn't affect callers.

The enforced 6-layer DAG in check-layers.sh includes hooks and routes as distinct layers, but the zone model collapses hooks into the engine zone and routes into the app zone — zone cohesion/coupling metrics therefore cannot surface hooks→services or routes→hooks violations; consider aligning zone boundaries with enforced layer boundaries

The game-engine zone contains an implicit two-tier structure: pure logic files (no service imports) and React hook files (service consumers); these two tiers are not distinguished by zone boundaries, obscuring where the I/O boundary actually sits within the zone

app-shell → hooks is the only outbound import direction from the shell; routes/play.tsx and routes/worlds.tsx import exclusively from ~/hooks, making the hooks layer a true anti-corruption layer between the UI entry point and domain logic

Engine pure-logic files have zero imports from services — all 9 cross-zone service imports come from hook files inside the same zone; the engine itself is fully side-effect-free, which is a stronger isolation guarantee than the zone-level coupling score implies

Two hook files import directly from '~/services/persistence' rather than the barrel '~/services', bypassing the public API surface that services/index.ts is designed to enforce; all consumers should go through the barrel

The app-shell zone has no co-located tests validating its own import contracts. The hooks-only import rule for route files is enforced by tools outside the zone (check-layers.sh, zone-boundaries.test.ts). A misconfigured route added by a contributor unfamiliar with the layer rules will not surface a failure until CI runs the external script, rather than failing a fast local unit test adjacent to the offending file.

arc-geometry is consumed independently by both the engine zone and the rainbow-arc-component zone. This fan-out means the geometry module's public API has two callers with no intermediary, so a signature change propagates to two zones simultaneously. As the geometry module grows, documenting and freezing its exported API surface becomes load-bearing for zone stability.

The 6-layer DAG contract lives exclusively in an unstructured shell script; layer renames or path convention changes cause silent enforcement gaps rather than explicit failures — extract the layer definitions into a machine-readable config shared by check-layers.sh and zone-boundaries.test.ts

The game-engine zone directly imports arc-geometry (engine→geometry edge) while also importing rainbow-arc-component (engine→components edge), which itself wraps the same geometry. If the direct geometry import is used for any rendering or layout purpose rather than pure game-state calculation, the engine is performing presentation work that should be delegated entirely to the component abstraction, violating the geometry→component→engine layering that the rainbow-arc zones were designed to enforce.

The hooks barrel (hooks/index.ts) is a curated export surface but no enforcement test asserts that every hook file in the hooks directory is re-exported through it. A developer adding a new hook and importing it via direct path rather than the barrel silently bypasses the documented public API contract without any lint, script, or test failure.

The engine→components import direction is enforced at the broad layer level by check-layers.sh but no fine-grained assertion prevents the rainbow-arc-component zone from importing game-engine zone internals, which would introduce a zone-level cycle. As both zones grow, the risk of an accidental reverse import increases without a targeted boundary test.

Direct imports from '~/services/persistence' by useGameSession.ts and useWorldSession.ts are a double violation: they bypass the barrel public API AND originate from files misclassified into the wrong zone — fixing zone classification alone will not fix the bypass, both must be corrected together

The engine barrel re-exports all arc-geometry symbols, creating an undocumented alias: `import { computeArcProgress } from '~/engine'` and `import { computeArcProgress } from '~/geometry/rainbow-arc'` resolve to identical code. This makes the engine barrel appear to own geometry logic it merely proxies. Remove the re-exports from the engine barrel to make the geometry module the sole canonical import source.

check-layers.sh line 12 documents only one of the two constraints enforced for the components layer — it mentions 'routes' but silently omits 'services'. A developer reading only the header comment block (lines 5–12) will have an incomplete picture of what is enforced. Update line 12 to: '- components/ must NOT import from routes/ or services/'.

eslint.config.ts claims to be the sole enforcement mechanism but check-layers.sh enforces the same rules — if ESLint is truly the single source of truth, check-layers.sh is redundant and should be documented as a secondary smoke-check rather than an independent enforcer; if both are intentional, eslint.config.ts line 6 should be corrected to say 'primary mechanism' rather than 'ONE AND ONLY'.
